$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}-2\kappa_{a}\right)\cdot e^{-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]=0. $$

By Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}-2\kappa_{a}\right)\cdot e^{-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}-2\kappa_{a}\right)^{2}\right]\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-2y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]}. $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-2y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\frac{2\|\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}\|^{2}}{n}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\frac{2\|\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}\|^{2}}{n}}\right]. $$

Further,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=2}^{p}\tilde{\beta}_{i}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\|\tilde{\beta}\|^{2}-\frac{1}{n}\tilde{\beta}_{1}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\|^{2}-\frac{1}{n}(\frac{\beta^{\top}}{\|\beta\|}\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}})^{2} \displaystyle\xrightarrow{a.s.} \displaystyle\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}+\left(\alpha_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}\gamma^{2}-\frac{(\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma^{2})^{2}}{\gamma^{2}}=\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}. $$

Thus we have

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\frac{2\|\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}\|^{2}}{n}}\right]=e^{2\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}}=O(1). $$

Moreover, we have

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}-2\kappa_{a}\right)^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

Thus we have shown

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}\cdot e^{-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[2\kappa_{a}e^{-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]. $$

As a result,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{1}}\cdot e^{-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[2\kappa_{a}e^{-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\kappa_{a}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{\frac{\|\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}\|^{2}}{2n}}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right]=2\kappa_{a}e^{\frac{1}{2}\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}}. $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}z_{i1}y_{i}\mid\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{r_{a}}{2}\cdot 2e_{\gamma,0}\cdot 2\kappa_{a}+\frac{r_{a}}{2}\cdot 2e^{\frac{\left(\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma\right)^{2}}{2}}e_{\gamma,-\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma}\cdot 2\kappa_{a}e^{\frac{1}{2}\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}}+o(1) \displaystyle=2\kappa\left(e_{\gamma,0}+e^{\frac{\left(\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma\right)^{2}+\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}}{2}}e_{\gamma,-\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma}\right)+o(1), $$

which implies

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}z_{i1}y_{i}\right] \displaystyle=2\kappa\left(e_{\gamma,0}+e^{\frac{\left(\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma\right)^{2}+\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}}{2}}e_{\gamma,-\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma}\right)+o(1). $$

We then find the limit of

$$ \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)\right]. $$

Similar to the previous argument, we can treat $\hat{\beta}_{S_{b}}$ as a deterministic vector. Note that

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}{A_{i}y_{i}}\right)\right] \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}e^{-z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}e^{-z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}}\right)\right]+\kappa. $$

Further, for any $i\neq j,\;i,j\in S_{a}$ , by symmetry of $y_{i}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[A_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{k\in S_{a}}A_{k}y_{k}y_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}{A_{j}y_{j}}e^{-z_{j}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[y_{i}^{\top}\left(y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}+\sum_{k\neq i}A_{k}y_{k}y_{k}^{\top}\right)^{-1}{A_{j}y_{j}}e^{-z_{j}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}}\right]=0. $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}{A_{i}y_{i}}e^{-z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[A_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}{A_{i}y_{i}}e^{-z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle r_{a}\mathbb{E}\left[A_{1}y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}{A_{1}y_{1}}e^{-z_{11}\tilde{\beta}_{1}-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{r_{a}}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[y_{1}^{\top}\left(y_{1}y_{1}^{\top}+\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}{y_{1}}e^{-w_{11}\tilde{\beta}_{1}-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{r_{a}}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-w_{11}\tilde{\beta}_{1}}\right]\mathbb{E}\left[y_{1}^{\top}\left(y_{1}y_{1}^{\top}+\sum_{j\in S_{a},j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}{y_{1}}e^{-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{r_{a}}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-w_{11}\tilde{\beta}_{1}}\right]\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-y_{1}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\frac{y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}{y_{1}}}{1+y_{1}^{\top}\left(\sum_{j\neq 1}A_{j}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\right)^{-1}{y_{1}}}\right]\quad\text{(Sherman\textendash Morrison)}. $$

Since

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-w_{11}\tilde{\beta}_{1}}\right]=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[e^{-z_{11}\tilde{\beta}_{1}}\mid A_{1}=1\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\sqrt{n}z\tilde{\beta}_{1}/\sqrt{n}}\cdot p\left(A_{1}=1\mid z_{11}=z\right)\cdot p\left(z_{11}=z\right)dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\sqrt{n}z\tilde{\beta}_{1}/\sqrt{n}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+e^{-z\|\beta\|}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{nz^{2}}{2}}dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-z\tilde{\beta}_{1}/\sqrt{n}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+e^{-z\|\beta\|/\sqrt{n}}}e^{-\frac{z^{2}}{2}}dz \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{e^{-z\tilde{\beta}_{1}/\sqrt{n}}}{1+e^{-z\|\beta\|/\sqrt{n}}}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{e^{-\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma z}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}\right]=2\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{1+e^{-\gamma(z-\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma)}}\right]e^{\frac{(\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma)^{2}}{2}}=2e^{\frac{\left(\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma\right)^{2}}{2}}q_{\gamma,-\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma}, $$

We have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\kappa+r_{a}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{e^{-\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma z}}{1+e^{-\gamma z}}\right]\cdot 2\kappa_{a}e^{\frac{1}{2}\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}}=2\kappa\left(\frac{1}{2}+e^{\frac{\left(\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma\right)^{2}+\kappa_{b}\left(\sigma_{b}^{*}\right)^{2}}{2}}q_{\gamma,-\alpha_{b}^{*}\gamma}\right). $$

We then show

$$ \text{Var}\left(\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}\frac{A_{i}y_{i}}{\sigma\left(z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}\right)}\right)\right)=o(1). $$

We know $\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}{A_{i}y_{i}}\right)$ converges to some constant. Furthermore, uniform integrability holds for the sequence. Therefore we only need to show

$$ \text{Var}\left(\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}{A_{i}y_{i}e^{-z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}}}\right)\right)=o(1). $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}{A_{i}y_{i}e^{-z_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{a}}{A_{i}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}\cdot e^{-z_{i1}\tilde{\beta}_{1}}\right) \displaystyle\sim \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}\cdot e^{-w_{i1}\tilde{\beta}_{1}}\right). $$

For all $i,j\in\{1,2,\ldots,\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor\}$ , define

$$ l_{i}=e^{-w_{i1}\tilde{\beta}_{1}},\quad T=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\right), $$

$$ T^{(l_{j})}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left({y_{j}e^{y_{j}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{j}^{{}^{\prime}}+\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\right), $$

$$ T^{(y_{j})}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\right). $$

Since $y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n_{a}},l_{1},l_{2},\ldots,l_{n_{a}}$ are independent, by Efron–Stein inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{Var}(T)\leq\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}\left(T-T^{(l_{i})}\right)^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}\left(T-T^{(y_{j})}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle=O(n)\mathbb{E}\left[\left(T-T^{(l_{1})}\right)^{2}\right]+O(n)\mathbb{E}\left[\left(T-T^{(y_{1})}\right)^{2}\right]. $$

Define $\tilde{n}_{a}=\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor.$ Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(T-T^{(l_{1})}\right)^{2}\right]=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}e^{y_{j}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\right)^{2}\cdot\left(l_{j}-l_{j}^{{}^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{2}e^{2y_{j}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\cdot\left(l_{j}-l_{j}^{{}^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{4}\right]\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[e^{4y_{j}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}\cdot\left(l_{j}-l_{j}^{\prime}\right)^{4}\right]} \displaystyle= \displaystyle O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{4}\right]}. $$

Thus in order to show

$$ O(n)\mathbb{E}\left[\left(T-T^{\left(l_{1}\right)}\right)^{2}\right]=o(1), $$

we only need to show

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{4}\right]=o(n^{2}). $$

By Sherman–Morrison formula, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}=\frac{\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\leq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}}{1+y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\leq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}} \displaystyle=O(1)\cdot\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}. $$

Thus we only need to show

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{4}\right]=o(n^{2}). $$

In fact, we only need to show

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}=o(1)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

Since

$$ \displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{a}}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j} \displaystyle=y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}+\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}, $$

and

$$ y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}=O(1)\quad\text{a.s.}, $$

we only need to show

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}=o(1)\quad\text{a.s.} $$

By symmetry the expectation of the left hand side is 0. Hence we only need to show

$$ \frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-2}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\tilde{n}_{a},i\neq j}y_{i}\right)\right]=O(1). $$

Thus we have proved

$$ O(n)\mathbb{E}\left[\left(T-T^{\left(l_{1}\right)}\right)^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

Next we show

$$ O(n)\mathbb{E}\left[\left(T-T^{\left(y_{1}\right)}\right)^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle T-T^{\left(y_{1}\right)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)+\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}e^{y_{j}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{j} \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left[\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}-\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right] \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\right). $$

Thus we only need to show

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{n}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right]=o(n^{-1}), \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left[\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}-\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right]\right.\right. \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left.\left.\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right]=o(n^{-1}). $$

First we show

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right]=o\left(1\right). $$

Since

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(y_{i}e^{y_{j}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{j}\right)=o(1)\quad\text{a.s.}, $$

we only need to show

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

By Sherman–Morrison,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\frac{1}{y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}}. $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle C\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\right)^{2}\right]+o(1) \displaystyle\text{ for some constant }C \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{C}{n^{2}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-2}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\right] \displaystyle+ \displaystyle o(1)=o(1). $$

Finally we show

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\Big)^{\top}\Big[\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\Big)^{-1}-\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\Big)^{-1}\Big] \displaystyle\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\Big)\Big)^{2}\Big]=o(1). $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left[\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}-\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right] \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left[\frac{\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}}{1+y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}}\right] \displaystyle\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle C\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j} \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}^{\top}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}+o(1)\quad\text{ for some constant }C. $$

Since

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right]=0, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right]^{2}\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}y_{j}^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\right. \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left.\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)\right] \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n^{1.5}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-2}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)\right]=o(1), $$

we know

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}=o(1)\quad\text{a.s.}, $$

which implies

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{4}\right]=o(1). $$

Similarly we can show

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{n}}\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}^{\top}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}l_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\right\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}y_{j}\right)^{4}\right]=o(1). $$

By Cauchy-Schwarz, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}\Big)^{\top}\Big[\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\Big)^{-1}-\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\Big)^{-1}\Big] \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\Big(\sum_{1\leq i\leq\lfloor\frac{n_{a}}{2}\rfloor,i\neq j}{y_{i}e^{y_{i}^{\top}\tilde{\beta}_{2:p}}}l_{i}\Big)\Big)^{2}\Big]=o(1). $$

This completes the proof.

Thus

$$ \displaystyle a^{\top}(O-Q)b=\frac{1}{1-\text{Tr}(VU^{-1})}a^{\top}U^{-1}VU^{-1}b \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\right)^{-1}\cdot\left[a^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)\right]}{1-\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\right)^{-1}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)} \displaystyle\cdot \displaystyle\left[b^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)\right]. $$

### F.2 Proof of Lemma C.2

\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}\begin{bmatrix}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x^{2}_{i1}&\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top}\\

C&D\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}\\

$$ C=-B(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top})^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}, $$

$$ D=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}-(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x^{2}_{i1})^{-1}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i})(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i})^{\top}\right)^{-1}. $$

where

$$ \displaystyle T_{1}= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x^{2}_{i1}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top})^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}\right)^{2} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}A_{i}\sqrt{n}x_{i1}\right)^{2}}{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}A_{i}\left(\sqrt{n}x_{i1}\right)^{2}-(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top})\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i})}, $$

$$ \displaystyle T_{2}= \displaystyle\frac{2}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}\right)C^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-\frac{2B}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle-2B\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}\sqrt{n}x_{i1}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}A_{i}y_{i}\right), $$

$$ \displaystyle T_{3}= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}-(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x^{2}_{i1})^{-1}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i})(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i})^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle{\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}\right)}+\frac{8\kappa^{2}e_{\gamma,0}^{2}}{1-2\kappa}\quad\text{(Due to lemma \ref{diff_lemma_1})}. $$

By applying the weak law for triangular arrays similarly as in the proof of Lemma D.4, we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}A_{i}\sqrt{n}x_{i1}\xrightarrow{p}e_{\gamma,0},\quad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}A_{i}\left(\sqrt{n}x_{i1}\right)^{2}\xrightarrow{p}\frac{1}{2}. $$

Next we find the limit of $T_{2}$ . We know

Further, we have

$$ \displaystyle B=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}^{2}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}y_{i}y_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i1}y_{i}\right)^{-1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}-\frac{p}{n}}+o_{p}(1)=\frac{2}{1-2\kappa}+o_{p}(1). $$

Hence

$$ T_{3}=\kappa+\frac{8\kappa^{2}e_{\gamma}^{2}}{1-2\kappa}+o_{p}(1). $$

Plugging the results into equation (45), we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}x_{i}\right)= \displaystyle\frac{2e_{\gamma}^{2}}{1-2\kappa}-\frac{8\kappa e_{\gamma}^{2}}{1-2\kappa}+\kappa+\frac{8r^{2}e_{\gamma}^{2}}{1-2\kappa}+o_{p}(1) \displaystyle=\kappa+2e_{\gamma,0}^{2}(1-2\kappa)+o_{p}(1), $$

### F.3 Proof of Lemma C.3

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\left(\frac{A_{j}x_{j}}{\sigma\left(x_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}\right)}-x_{j}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{j\in S_{a}}\left(\frac{A_{j}x_{j}}{\sigma\left(x_{j}^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}\right)}\right) \displaystyle- \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}x_{i}\right)^{\top}\left(\sum_{i\in S_{b}}A_{i}x_{i}x_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\sum_{j\in S_{a}}x_{j}\right). $$

## G Proof of Theorem 3.4

In this section, we first state the full result of Theorem 3.4. To this end, we need some additional notation.

Fix any ridge penalty parameter $\lambda>0$ . For any $i=1,2,3$ , let $\left(\alpha_{i}^{(\lambda)},\sigma_{i}^{(\lambda)},\lambda_{i}^{(\lambda)}\right)$ be the solution to the system of equations (4.12) in [107], where the covariates are of dimension $n_{i}\times p$ with i.i.d. entries $\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\frac{1}{n_{i}}\right)$ , the signal strength is $\gamma^{2}$ , and the ridge penalty parameter is $\lambda$ . Moreover, define

$$ \tilde{\alpha}_{i}^{(\lambda)}=\alpha_{i}^{(\lambda)}\cdot\frac{\kappa_{a}-\lambda\lambda_{a}^{\left(\lambda\right)}}{\kappa_{a}},\quad\tilde{\sigma}_{i}^{(\lambda)}=\sigma_{i}^{(\lambda)}\cdot\frac{\kappa_{a}-\lambda\lambda_{a}^{\left(\lambda\right)}}{\kappa_{a}},\quad\tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{(\lambda)}=\lambda_{i}^{(\lambda)}. $$

Then the asymptotic variance $\left(\sigma_{cf}^{(\lambda)}\right)^{2}$ in Theorem 3.4 is the same as the expression for $\sigma_{cf}^{2}$ in Theorem 3.3, except that $(\alpha_{i}^{*},\sigma_{i}^{*},\lambda_{i}^{*})$ is replaced by $\left(\tilde{\alpha}_{i}^{(\lambda/r_{i})},\tilde{\sigma}_{i}^{(\lambda/r_{i})},\tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{(\lambda/r_{i})}\right)\;\;\forall i\in\{1,2,3\}$ .

The proof of Theorem 3.4 can be obtained by modifying the proof of Theorem 3.3. In particular, we only need to modify the lemmas involved in the proof of Theorem 3.3 that use properties of MLE for logistic regression models.

#### Lemma G.1.

Fix any ridge penalty parameter $\lambda>0$ . Fix any $(a,b,c)$ , a permutation of $(1,2,3)$ . Assume the setting described in section 2. Let $x\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ be any sample in $S_{c}$ . Then the random vector $\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x^{\top}\beta\\ x^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}\end{array}\right)$ converges in distribution to a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and variance $\Sigma$ , where

$$ \Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}\gamma^{2}&\tilde{\alpha}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}_{a}\gamma^{2}\\
\tilde{\alpha}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}_{a}\gamma^{2}&\quad\kappa_{a}\left(\tilde{\sigma}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}_{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\tilde{\alpha}_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}\right)^{2}\gamma^{2}\end{bmatrix}. $$

Conditioned on $S_{a},S_{b}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x^{\top}\beta\\
x^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}\end{array}\right)\sim N\left(\mathbf{0},\frac{1}{n}\begin{bmatrix}\|\beta\|^{2}&\beta^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}\\
\beta^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}&\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}\|^{2}\end{bmatrix}\right). $$

By assumption

$$ \frac{\|\beta\|^{2}}{n}\rightarrow\gamma^{2}. $$

Note that $\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}$ is estimated from $S_{a}$ , where $X_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{a}\times p}$ with i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n})$ . Define

$$ \beta^{{}^{\prime}}=\sqrt{r_{a}}\beta,\quad\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{{}^{\prime}}=\sqrt{r_{a}}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)},\quad X_{a}^{{}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{r_{a}}}X_{a} $$

Then $X_{a}^{{}^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{a}\times p}$ with i.i.d. entries $\sim N(0,\frac{1}{n_{a}})$ , and $X_{a}\beta=X_{a}^{{}^{\prime}}\beta^{{}^{\prime}},X_{a}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}=X_{a}^{{}^{\prime}}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{{}^{\prime}}$ . Moreover,

$$ \frac{\|\beta^{{}^{\prime}}\|^{2}}{n_{a}}=\frac{r_{a}\|\beta\|^{2}}{n_{a}}=\frac{\|\beta\|^{2}}{n}\rightarrow\gamma^{2}. $$

According to Chapter 4, Result 1 in [107],

$$ \frac{1}{p}(\beta^{{}^{\prime}})^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{{}^{\prime}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}\frac{\alpha_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}}{p}\left(\beta^{\prime}\right)^{\top}\beta^{\prime}\cdot\frac{\kappa_{a}-\lambda\lambda_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}}{\kappa_{a}}. $$

This implies

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n}\beta^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}=\alpha_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}\gamma^{2}\cdot\frac{\kappa_{a}-\lambda\lambda_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}}{\kappa_{a}}\quad\text{almost surely.} $$

Moreover, applying Chapter 4, Result 1 in [107] with $\psi(t,u)=t^{2}$ yields

$$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{{}^{\prime}}\|^{2}}{p}=\left[(\sigma_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})})^{2}+(\alpha_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})})^{2}\frac{r_{a}\gamma^{2}}{\kappa}\right]\cdot\left(\frac{\kappa_{a}-\lambda\lambda_{a}^{\left(\lambda/r_{a}\right)}}{\kappa_{a}}\right)^{2}\quad\text{almost surely.} $$

Thus

$$ \frac{\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}\|^{2}}{n}=\frac{\|\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{\prime}\|^{2}}{p}\cdot\frac{p}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{r_{a}}\xrightarrow{a.s.}\left[\kappa_{a}(\sigma_{a}^{\left(\lambda/r_{a}\right)})^{2}+(\alpha_{a}^{\left(\lambda/r_{a}\right)})^{2}\gamma^{2}\right]\cdot\left(\frac{\kappa_{a}-\lambda\lambda_{a}^{\left(\lambda/r_{a}\right)}}{\kappa_{a}}\right)^{2}. $$

Hence we know

$$ \displaystyle\left(\begin{array}[]{c}x^{\top}\beta\\
x^{\top}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}\end{array}\right)\xrightarrow{d}N\left(\mathbf{0},\begin{bmatrix}\gamma^{2}&\tilde{\alpha}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}_{a}\gamma^{2}\\
\tilde{\alpha}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}_{a}\gamma^{2}&\quad\kappa_{a}\left(\tilde{\sigma}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}_{a}\right)^{2}+\left(\tilde{\alpha}_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}\right)^{2}\gamma^{2}\end{bmatrix}\right), $$

which does not depend on $S_{a},S_{b}$ . This completes the proof of the lemma. ∎

Below we state the properties of MLE for logistic regression models that are used in the proof of Theorem 3.3, and show how they can be modified to prove Theorem 3.4.

(i) The proof of Lemma B.3 and C.6 uses the following property:

$$ \frac{1}{n}\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{T}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}=\alpha_{a}^{*}\alpha_{c}^{*}\gamma^{2}+o(1)\quad\text{a.s.}\quad\forall a,c\in\{1,2,3\}. $$

Similar to the proof of Lemma G.1, with an extension of Chapter 4, Result 1 in [107], we can show

$$ \frac{1}{n}\left(\hat{\beta}_{S_{a}}^{(\lambda)}\right)^{T}\hat{\beta}_{S_{c}}^{(\lambda)}=\tilde{\alpha}_{a}^{(\lambda/r_{a})}\tilde{\alpha}_{c}^{(\lambda/r_{c})}\gamma^{2}+o(1)\quad\text{a.s.}\quad\forall a,c\in\{1,2,3\}. $$

(ii) The proof of Lemma C.6 and C.8 uses Lemma 21 in [107]. Since the ridge penalty is strongly convex, its Hessian is positive. Thus Lemma 16 in [107] still holds if we replace the negative log-likelihood with the sum of the negative log-likelihood and the ridge penalty. ## Abstract

We address the challenge of constructing valid confidence intervals and sets in problems of prediction across multiple environments. We investigate two types of coverage suitable for these problems, extending the jackknife and split-conformal methods to show how to obtain distribution-free coverage in such non-traditional, potentially hierarchical data-generating scenarios. We demonstrate a novel resizing method to adapt to problem difficulty, which applies both to existing approaches for predictive inference and the methods we develop; this reduces prediction set sizes using limited information from the test environment, a key to the methods’ practical performance, which we evaluate through neurochemical sensing and species classification datasets. Our contributions also include extensions for settings with non-real-valued responses, a theory of consistency for predictive inference in these general problems, and insights on the limits of conditional coverage

## 1 Introduction

In the predictive inference problem, a statistician observes a training sample $\{(X_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ of size $n$ and wishes to predict the unknown value of $Y_{n+1}$ at a test point $X_{n+1}$ , where in the classical setting, $\{(X_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n+1}$ are exchangeable random variables. Vovk et al.’s conformal prediction [35] addresses this problem, even in finite sample and distribution-free settings, constructing a prediction band $\widehat{C}$ such that $\widehat{C}(X_{n+1})$ covers $Y_{n+1}$ with a desired probability on average over the draw $(X_{n+1},Y_{n+1})$ .

In contemporary problems, however, the statistician rarely observes data from a single set of identically distributed training examples, instead receiving data implicitly or explicitly arising from multiple environments. For instance, a neuroscientist investigating diseases of the nervous system may use multiple electrodes to measure neurotransmitter levels, with a goal to predict these levels at future time points. Variations—whether in voltage potentials, experimental conditions, build of the electrode, or otherwise—yield data from different electrodes that follow distinct distributions [25]. To understand the neurobiological underpinnings of decision making, the statistician must leverage information from multiple electrodes to develop a prediction model that alleviates spurious electrode-to-electrode variations. Additionally, even in cases in which one tries to exactly replicate data generating methodology, distribution shift means that prediction methods lose substantial accuracy [27, 30]. We investigate and develop methodology for constructing prediction intervals for such multi-environment problems.

### 1.1 Problem Setting

Data from multiple environments should improve predictions on a target only if the training and test data share common characteristics. We begin by considering a framework of hierarchical sampling [26, 22, 12], where one assumes that data from different environments arise from a common hierarchical model. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a set of distributions on $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$ , where $\mathcal{Y}$ is the outcome/response space and $\mathcal{X}$ is the space of covariates, and $\mu$ denote a probability distribution on $\mathcal{P}\times\mathbb{N}$ . Consider a sequence of exchangeable pairs generated from $\mu$ ,

$$ (P_{XY}^{1},n_{1}),\ldots,(P_{XY}^{m+1},n_{m+1}), $$

where in training we observe i.i.d. samples

$$ (X^{i},Y^{i})\coloneqq\{X_{j}^{i},Y_{j}^{i}\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}},~{}~{}~{}(X^{i}_{j%
},Y_{j}^{i})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm iid}}{{\sim}}P_{XY}^{i}, $$

for $j\in[n_{i}]$ and $i\in[m]$ , treating $P^{i}_{XY}$ as the $i$ th environment. In the test, we observe an i.i.d. sample $\{X_{j}^{m+1}\}_{j=1}^{n_{m+1}}$ generated from the marginal distribution on $X$ according to the $(m+1)$ st $P_{XY}^{m+1}$ , and we wish to construct confidence sets for the unknown responses $\{Y_{j}^{m+1}\}_{j=1}^{n_{m+1}}$ with valid coverage. We depart from the traditional predictive inference literature in the sense that individual observations need not be exchangeable. Instead, hierarchical sampling assumes that within each environment, the observations are exchangeable, and the environments themselves are exchangeable as well. This weaker assumption allows addressing scenarios where the data may exhibit variations across different environments, but defining valid coverage requires careful consideration.

We consider two coverage notions for multi-environment settings. The first considers properties close to those conformal prediction provides [35, 2], relying on the i.i.d. sampling from $P^{i}$ in the model (1)–(2): we seek $\widehat{C}$ covering a single new example with a prescribed probability.

#### Definition 1.1.

A confidence set mapping $\widehat{C}:\mathcal{X}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{Y}$ provides $1-\alpha$ hierarchical coverage in the setting (1) if for the single observation $(X_{1}^{m+1},Y_{1}^{m+1})\sim P^{m+1}_{XY}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(Y_{1}^{m+1}\in\widehat{C}(X_{1}^{m+1})\right)\geq 1-\alpha. $$

Dunn et al. [12] and Lee et al. [22] both adopt the guarantee (3) as a notion of coverage.

Instead of this marginal guarantee over a single observation from the new environment $m+1$ and the i.i.d. within environment setting (2)—and given that we expect to collect multiple observations from each environment—it is also natural to consider coverage notions over entire new samples. Thus, we consider data generation where only the full samples are exchangeable: let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on $\mathcal{E}\times\mathbb{N}$ , where $\mathcal{E}$ is a collection of environments; then we receive exchangeable samples

$$ (E_{i},n_{i})\sim\mu~{}~{}\mbox{and}~{}~{}(X^{i},Y^{i})\coloneqq\{X_{j}^{i},Y_%
{j}^{i}\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}}, $$

where $(X^{i},Y^{i})$ is generated via a Markov kernel from $\mathcal{E}\times\mathbb{N}$ to $(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})^{n_{i}}$ . This makes no assumptions about the relationships between individual observations $(X_{j}^{i},Y_{j}^{i})$ , so we consider a stronger coverage property:

#### Definition 1.2.

A confidence set mapping $\widehat{C}:\mathcal{X}\rightrightarrows\mathcal{Y}$ provides distribution-free level $(\alpha,\delta)$ -coverage in the setting (4) if

$$ \mathbb{P}\bigg{(}\frac{1}{n_{m+1}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{m+1}}1\!\left\{Y_{j}^{m+1}%
\in\widehat{C}(X_{j}^{m+1})\right\}\geq 1-\alpha\bigg{)}\geq 1-\delta. $$

That is, $\widehat{C}$ covers a $1-\alpha$ fraction of observed examples in the new environment with probability at least $1-\delta$ .

### 1.2 Main Contributions

Our main contributions include the following.

- 1. We introduce the multi-environment jackknife and split conformal methods (Algorithms 2.1 and 2.2, respectively). Theorems 1 and 2.3 establish that these provide distribution-free level $(\alpha,\delta)$ -coverage (5) when the response space $\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}$ . These algorithms straightforwardly extend (see Algorithms 3.1 and 3.1) to general response spaces $\mathcal{Y}$ , and they continue to provide $(\alpha,\delta)$ -coverage (see Theorems 3.5 and 3.6 in Sec. 3).

- 2. We investigate the behavior of algorithms targeting $(\alpha,\delta)$ -coverage (5) alongside previous work on hierarchical conformal inference [22], evaluating methods on neurochemical sensing [25] and species classification [21, 7] data. Our experiments (Sec. 4) reveal that the multi-environment jackknife tends to yield smaller confidence sets than the split-conformal methodology when there are fewer training environments. Conversely, the multi-environment split conformal method demonstrates better performance when the number of training environments is large.

- 3. The experiments indicate that multi-environment algorithms can be conservative, and to mitigate this, we propose and evaluate a resizing method (Algorithm 5 in Sec. 5) to reduce the size of prediction sets given access to a limited amount of information from the test environment. This strategy appears to be useful for predictive inference more generally, including to hierarchical conformal prediction (HCP) [22], where it yields notable set size reductions.

- 4. We develop new consistency theory (see Theorems 6.15 and 6.18 in Sec. 6) for multi-environment predictive inference, showing how jackknife and split conformal methods produce consistent confidence sets.

- 5. We also touch briefly (see Section 7) on environment-conditional coverage; in analogy to standard single environment settings [34, 5], we show that conditional coverage is impossible, extending these ideas to reflect that environments may be discrete. Approximate environment-conditional coverage can, however, hold.

### 1.3 Related Work

Standard predictive inference methods include split-conformal [35, 24, 10, 29, 8, 9, 16] and modified jackknife procedures [6]. The current paper extends these to multi-environment problems. Split conformal prediction separates the data into a training and a calibration set, using the training data to fit a model and the calibration data to set a threshold for constructing prediction intervals. Since it only splits the data once, the method may sacrifice statistical efficiency for computational gains. Addressing this issue, jackknife-style procedures use all available data for training and calibration by fitting leave-one-out models, increasing computational cost for accuracy. Both methods require exchangeability of the entire observed data to ensure valid coverage, while multi-environment methods work under the weaker assumption that within (but not across) environments, observations are exchangeable, and the environments themselves are exchangeable.

Recognizing the challenges inherent in collecting data, implicitly or explicitly, across multiple environments, a recent literature considers conformal prediction under hierarchical models, assuming the multi-environment setting (1)–(2). Among these, Dunn et al. [12] and Lee et al. [22] study conformal prediction under hierarchical sampling and propose methods satisfying the marginal coverage guarantee (3), as well as a few other distribution-free guarantees, which may be a satisfying coverage guarantee for many applications. The $(\alpha,\delta)$ -coverage condition (5) requires coverage for multiple examples in the test environment simultaneously without assuming i.i.d. sampling within each environment, and it is unclear if existing multi-level conformal approaches satisfy it.

We define a fitting algorithm $\mathsf{A}$ to be a function that takes a collection of samples as input and outputs an element of $\mathcal{F}\subset\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ . To describe our algorithms formally, we introduce two quantile-type mappings, where for $v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ we let $v_{(1)}\leq v_{(2)}\leq\cdots\leq v_{(n)}$ be its order statistics.

The idea is simple: we repeatedly fit a predictor $\widehat{f}_{-i}$ to all environments except environment $i$ , then evaluate residuals on environment $i$ to gauge the variability of predicting on a new environment. We define $\widehat{f}=\mathsf{A}((X^{1},Y^{1}),\ldots,(X^{m},Y^{m}))$ to be the predictor we would fit given each sample $(X^{i},Y^{i})=\{(X_{j}^{i},Y_{j}^{i})\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}}$ , and consider the leave-one-out predictors

## 3 General confidence sets and extensions

To this point, we have described our algorithms for real-valued predictions, where confidence intervals $C(x)=[a,b]$ are most practicable. Here, we generalize the algorithms beyond regression, where the target space may not be the real line and the prediction sets may be asymmetric. We first present the general formulation and abstract algorithms. Subsequently, we specialize our construction to demonstrate implementation in a few cases of interest: (i) when we represent general target spaces $\mathcal{Y}$ and confidence sets by labels $y$ that suffer small loss under a prediction $f(x)$ , i.e., $\{y\in\mathcal{Y}\mid\ell(y,f(x))\leq\tau\}$ , and (ii) for quantile regression-type approaches, which allow asymmetric confidence sets in regression problems [28].

## 4 Real Data Examples

With the “basic” setting of the preceding sections, we move to real-data experiments to evaluate the methods; these methods motivate some of the extensions and further theory to come in the sequel.

### 4.1 Neurochemical Sensing

We apply our algorithms to the prediction of neurotransmitter concentration levels, with a specific focus on dopamine. Estimating dopamine levels in awake, functioning humans at a relatively high frequency is notoriously challenging, but because dopamine governs critical human behavior, understanding stimuli that maintain healthy dopamine levels is of crucial importance [20].

Scientists now have access to extensive lab generated multi-environment data that can aid in improving human dopamine level predictions [26, 4]. Scientists expose electrodes to various known dopamine concentrations and collect measurements of currents that pass through the electrodes at different voltage potentials (say $p$ different potentials). From each electrode, the scientist obtains a matrix, where each row records the different current levels in the electrode, when one changes its potential over a set of $p$ values while exposing it to a specific dopamine concentration level. For each electrode exposed to a certain concentration level, the scientist collects multiple $p$ -dimensional measurements across different time points. By changing the concentration over $\ell\geq 1$ distinct levels and collecting $t\gg 1$ observations at each level, the scientist obtains $n=\ell\times t$ observations, resulting in an $n\times p$ covariate matrix from each electrode. The $t$ measurements corresponding to each level may exhibit weak correlations, but since state-of-the-art scientific work in the area [26] treats these to be independent, we adopt this convention. Row outcomes thus measure the dopamine level that generated that row’s current values. Variations in electrode construction and the experimental setup under which measurements are obtained mean that the data from different electrodes follow different distributions.

To map this application to our setting, we consider each electrode to be one of our environments. We use data from multiple electrodes to train our algorithms, hoping that such multi-environment learning would create robust prediction models that generalize better when applied in a different context, e.g. while predicting dopamine levels on the human brain. The training data comprises 15 environments corresponding to $15$ electrodes. Each includes roughly 20,000 observations [26, 25]. of current measured in nanoamps (nA) collected at 1000 discrete voltage potentials. For each observation, the outcome is a measurement of nanomolar (nM) dopamine concentration. The outcomes lie in $[0,2000]$ , so we intersect our predictions with this range before producing intervals.

In each experiment, we select 5 environments at random for training and use the rest for testing. We train Algorithms 2.1 and 2.2 and examine their coverage on the test data under the $(\alpha,\delta)$ -coverage notion in Definition 1.2. We use ridge regression for the base model $\widehat{f}$ and leave-one-out cross validation for choosing the ridge parameter, repeating the experiment $100$ times and plotting the average coverage and the average set length (defined below).

For the $k$ th of 100 experiments, we let $\{e_{k,i}\}_{1\leq i\leq 5}$ and $\{e_{k,i}\}_{6\leq i\leq 15}$ denote the train and test environments, respectively. For $k\in[100],i\in[15]$ , we use $n_{k,i}$ to denote the sample size in environment $e_{k,i}$ and $\{X_{j}^{k,i},Y_{j}^{k,i}\}_{1\leq j\leq n_{k,i}}$ the observations. We define

## 5 Resizing residuals to reduce interval lengths

Our experimental results in Section 4 make clear that naive application of multi-environment algorithms often produces wide prediction intervals. The bottom plots in Figures 4.1 and 4.3 show that the average size of the confidence sets are particularly large when the input parameter $\delta$ is small. This conservativeness is a natural consequence of the constructions of the multi-environment confidence sets, just as Romano et al. [28] note that naive symmetric and uniform prediction intervals (i.e., those of the form $\widehat{C}(x)=[f(x)-\tau,f(x)+\tau]$ ) can be overly conservative as they must typically cover even values $X$ for which $Y$ is highly non-symmetric or has high variance. In our context, this presents when an environment $i$ has residual quantile $S_{1-\alpha}^{i}$ much larger than the rest—it is an outlier environment. For small $\delta$ , such outlier environments mostly determine the $1-\delta$ quantile of the training environments’ scores $S^{i}_{1-\alpha}$ , and consequently, these outlier training environments govern the size of the confidence set for test samples regardless of whether the test environment is outlying.

To mitigate this issue, we scale the residual quantiles by a resizing factor so that the adjusted quantiles (i) remain exchangeable, and (ii) are supported on a similar range for all environments. We compute the $1-\delta$ quantile of these adjusted residual quantiles. Finally, we multiply this $1-\delta$ quantile by the test environment’s resizing factor to construct valid confidence sets. This way, the constructed confidence set length remains small if the test environment is not an outlier. Since the probability of any environment being an outlier is small, the size of the constructed confidence set tends to be small on average.

The question therefore turns to finding an accurate strategy for constructing these resizing factors. One natural approach is—if they are available—to incorporate environmental covariates. If environmental covariates $e\in\mathcal{E}$ are available for each environment, then we can estimate resizing factors using them. (One could also incorporate these into the predictor $f:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{Y}$ via an expanded covariate $(X,e)$ .) Alternatively, we show that given access to a limited amount of labeled data from the test environment, one can indeed construct suitable resizing factors. We describe our strategy in the context of the multi-environment split conformal algorithm.

Suppose we observe $L^{m+1}$ labeled random examples from the test environment. As before, we partition the training environments into two sets $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ . Using data from environments in $D_{1}$ , we construct a nested confidence set $\{\widehat{C}_{\tau}\}_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}$ . We randomly select $L^{m+1}$ samples from each training environment and compute residuals for these samples using the $\{\widehat{C}_{\tau}\}_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}$ confidence sets. We then pick some quantile $\alpha_{0}$ close to 0, and compute the $1-\alpha_{0}$ quantile of these residuals as the resizing factor for each environment. As a result, the resizing factors for outlier environments tend to be large as desired. Empirically, we find that $\alpha_{0}=0.05$ works well for a reasonable range of input $\alpha$ . One can adapt this approach to any of multi-environment jackknife-minmax, hierarchical conformal prediction, or hierarchical jackknife+; Algorithm 5 shows how to do so for multi-environment split conformal prediction.

Algorithm 7: Resized Multi-environment Split Conformal Input: samples $\{X^{i}_{j},Y^{i}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n_{i}}$ , $i\in[m]$ , labeled samples $\{X_{j}^{m+1},Y_{j}^{m+1}\}_{j\in L^{m+1}}$ , confidence levels $\alpha,\delta$ , split ratio $\gamma$ , predictive set algorithm , resizing quantile $\alpha_{0}$ Randomly partition $[m]$ into $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ with $\frac{|D_{1}|}{m}=\gamma$ . set $\{\widehat{C}^{D_{1}}_{\tau}\}_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}=$ For $i\in D_{2}$ , 1. $$ s^{i}:=\widehat{q}_{|L^{i}|,\alpha_{0}}^{+}\left(\{R_{j}^{i}\}_{j\in L^{i}}% \right), $$

and resized residual quantiles

$$ S_{1-\alpha}^{i}=\widehat{q}_{n_{i},\alpha}^{+}\left(\left\{R_{j}^{i}/{s^{i}}% \right\}_{j\in[n_{i}]\setminus L^{i}}\right). $$

## 6 General Consistency Results

In this section, we develop a theory of consistency for the nested confidence sets in Section 3. We define consistency via convergence to a particular limiting confidence set mapping. When this confidence set is in some sense optimal, then our methods are consistent. To that end, we shall assume there is a fixed collection $\{C_{\tau}\}$ of nested confidence sets, and we let $E$ be a random environment drawn from the collection of possible environments $\mathcal{E}$ , letting $\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid E)$ denote the induced distribution conditional on $E$ . For a fixed $\alpha,\delta\in(0,1)$ , we define

$$ \displaystyle\tau^{\star}(\delta,\alpha) \displaystyle\coloneqq\inf\left\{\tau~{}\mbox{s.t.}~{}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{%
P}\left(Y\in C_{\tau}(X)\mid E\right)\geq 1-\alpha\right)\geq 1-\delta\right\}. $$

Thus, for the given confidence mappings $C=\{C_{\tau}\}$ , the value $\tau^{\star}(\delta,\alpha)$ yields the smallest confidence set providing $(\delta,\alpha)$ coverage (Definition 1.2) at a population level. Then for Algorithms 3.1 and 3.1 to be consistent, we must have the resulting confidence sets $\widehat{C}^{\textup{jk-mmx}}_{m,\alpha,\delta}$ and $\widehat{C}^{\textup{split}}_{m,\alpha,\delta}$ approach $C_{\tau^{\star}}$ in an appropriate sense.

### 6.1 Conditions and preliminary definitions

We require a few more definitions, providing examples as we state them. For a given nested confidence family $C=\{C_{\tau}\}$ , we define the coverage threshold

$$ \tau(x,y,C)\coloneqq\inf\left\{\tau\in\mathbb{R}\mid y\in C_{\tau}(x)\right\} $$

to be the smallest value $\tau$ such that $C_{\tau}(x)$ covers $y$ .

#### Example 6.10 (Coverage thresholds).

The coverage threshold (7) has straightforwardly computable values for most of the “standard” cases of confidence sets we consider. For the interval-based confidence set $C_{\tau}(x)=[f(x)-\tau,f(x)+\tau]$ , evidently $\tau(x,y,C)=|f(x)-y|$ . For the lower/upper sets we use in quantile regression (recall Section 3.2.2), where $C_{\tau}(x)=[l(x)-\tau,u(x)+\tau]$ , we have $\tau(x,y,C)=\max\{l(x)-y,y-u(x)\}$ , so that $\tau(X_{i}^{j},Y_{i}^{j},\widehat{C}^{-i})=R_{j}^{i}$ is simply the residual. For the generic loss-based set $C_{\tau}(x)=\{y\mid\ell(y,f(x))\leq\tau\}$ (recall Section 3.2.1), it is immediate that $\tau(x,y,C)=\ell(y,f(x))$ , and so once again we have equality with the residuals $R_{j}^{i}=\tau(X_{i}^{j},Y_{i}^{j},\widehat{C}^{-i})$ .

To discuss convergence of the estimators in general, we must address modes of quantile convergence, which we do at a generic level via convergence in distribution. To that end, for an $\mathbb{R}$ -valued random variable $Z$ , let

$$ \mathcal{L}(Z\mid P) $$

denote the induced probability law of $Z$ under the probability distribution $P$ . For example, letting $\widehat{P}^{i}$ be the empirical distribution of $(X_{j}^{i},Y_{j}^{i})_{j=1}^{n_{i}}$ , then the empirical distribution of the values $\tau(X_{j}^{i},Y_{j}^{i},\widehat{C}^{-i})$ becomes $\mathcal{L}(\tau(X,Y,\widehat{C}^{-i})\mid\widehat{P}^{i})$ . We recall the bounded Lipschitz metric between distributions $P$ and $Q$ ,

$$ \left\|{P-Q}\right\|_{\textup{BL}}\coloneqq\sup_{\left\|{f}\right\|_{\infty}%
\leq 1,\left\|{f}\right\|_{\textup{Lip}}\leq 1}\int f(dP-dQ), $$

noting that for any distribution $P$ on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , if $\widehat{P}_{n}$ denotes the empirical distribution of $Z_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm iid}}{{\sim}}P$ , $i=1,\ldots,n$ , then $\|{\widehat{P}_{n}-P}\|_{\textup{BL}}\mathop{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{% \rightarrow}}}0$ (see, e.g., van der Vaart and Wellner [33, Chs. 1.10–1.12]).

An essentially standard lemma relates convergence in the bounded Lipschitz metric to quantiles; for completeness we include a proof in Appendix C.1.

#### Lemma 6.11.

Let $Q$ be a distribution on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\alpha$ -quantile $\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}(Q)$ such that if $Z\sim Q$ , then

$$ Q(Z\leq\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}(Q)-u)<\alpha~{}~{}\mbox{and}~{}~{}Q(Z\leq\mathsf{Q}%
_{\alpha}(Q)+u)>\alpha $$

for all $u>0$ . Then the quantile mapping $\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}$ is continuous at $Q$ for the bounded-Lipschitz metric: for each $\epsilon>0$ , there exists $\delta>0$ such that $\left\|{P-Q}\right\|_{\textup{BL}}\leq\delta$ implies $|\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}(P)-\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha}(Q)|\leq\epsilon$ .

With these definitions, we make a few assumptions on the convergence of the estimated families of nested confidence sets. We will then revisit the major examples of confidence sets we have considered—the symmetric sets in the multi-environment jackknife-minmax (Section 2), the loss-based sets in Section 3.2.1, and the quantile-type sets in Section 3.2.2—and show natural sufficient conditions for the assumptions to hold.

The first two relate to consistency and continuity of the nested confidence sets.

#### Assumption 1.a.

Fix environment $i$ . As $n\to\infty$ ,

$$ \left\|{\mathcal{L}(\tau(X,Y,C)\mid P^{i})-\mathcal{L}(\tau(X,Y,\widehat{C}^{-%
i})\mid\widehat{P}^{i})}\right\|_{\textup{BL}}\mathop{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a%
.s.}}{{\rightarrow}}}0, $$

where $\widehat{C}^{-i}=\{\widehat{C}_{\tau}^{-i}\}_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}$ is defined in Algorithm 3.1.

#### Assumption 1.b.

Fix any validation environment $E=i$ . As $n\rightarrow\infty$ ,

$$ \left\|{\mathcal{L}(\tau(X,Y,C)\mid P^{i})-\mathcal{L}(\tau(X,Y,\widehat{C}^{D%
_{1}})\mid\widehat{P}^{i})}\right\|_{\textup{BL}}\mathop{\stackrel{{%
\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{\rightarrow}}}0, $$

where $\widehat{C}^{D_{1}}=\{\widehat{C}^{D_{1}}_{\tau}\}_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}$ is defined in Algorithm 3.1.

#### Assumption 2.c.

Let $\lambda$ be a measure on $\mathcal{Y}$ , fix $\tau^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}$ , and let $\epsilon>0$ . Define the (random) subsets

$$ B^{i}_{n,\tau}\coloneqq\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}~{}\mbox{s.t.}~{}\lambda\left(%
\widehat{C}_{\tau}^{-i}(x)\triangle C_{\tau^{\star}}(x)\right)\geq\epsilon%
\right\}, $$

indexed by $n\in\mathbb{N},\tau\in\mathbb{R}$ , and $i\leq m$ , of $\mathcal{X}$ . Let $\tau(n)$ be such that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\tau(n)=\tau^{\star}$ . Then for suitably slowly growing $m=m(n)\to\infty$ , the $X$ -measure of $B_{n,\tau}\coloneqq\cup_{i=1}^{m}B_{n,\tau}^{i}$ satisfies $\lim_{n\to\infty}P_{X}(B_{n,\tau(n)})=0$ with probability 1.

#### Assumption 2.d.

Let $\lambda$ be a measure on $\mathcal{Y}$ , fix $\tau^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}$ , and let $\epsilon>0$ . Define the (random) subsets

$$ B^{\textup{split}}_{n,\tau}\coloneqq\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}~{}\mbox{s.t.}~{}%
\lambda\left(\widehat{C}^{D_{1}}_{\tau}(X)\triangle C_{\tau^{\star}}(X)\right)%
\geq\epsilon\right\}, $$

indexed by $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$ , of $\mathcal{X}$ . Let $\tau(n)$ be such that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\tau(n)=\tau^{\star}$ . Then the $X$ -measure of $B^{\textup{split}}_{n,\tau}$ satisfies $\lim_{n\to\infty}P_{X}(B^{\textup{split}}_{n,\tau(n)})=0$ with probability 1.

These give a type of consistency of the confidence set mappings $\widehat{C}^{-i}$ and $\widehat{C}^{D_{1}}$ to $C$ .

#### 6.1.1 Examples realizing the assumptions

A few examples may make it clearer that we expect Assumptions 1.a and 2.c to hold. Similar arguments apply for Assumptions 1.b and 2.d, and thus are omitted. Throughout the examples, we make the standing assumption that if $\pi$ is the (prior) distribution on environments and $P_{X}=\int P^{e}_{X}d\pi(e)$ is the marginal distribution over $X$ , then

$$ \sup_{e\in\mathcal{E}}D_{\chi^{2}}\left({P^{e}_{X}}|\!|{P_{X}}\right)\leq\rho_%
{\chi^{2}}^{2}<\infty. $$

In this case, for any $g:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\int g(dP^{e}-dP)\right|=\left|\int g\left(\frac{dP^{e}}{dP%
}-1\right)dP\right| \displaystyle\qquad\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{P}[g^{2}]}\sqrt{D_{\chi^{2}}\left({P^%
{e}}|\!|{P}\right)}\leq\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{P}[g^{2}]}\rho_{\chi^{2}}; $$

in particular, $|P^{e}(A)-P(A)|\leq\sqrt{P(A)}\rho_{\chi^{2}}$ for $A\subset\mathcal{X}$ .

We now give three examples: regression, quantile regression, and (multiclass) logistic regression, and for each we provide a simple sufficient condition for Assumptions 1.a and 2.c to hold. For all three examples, the sufficient condition assumes the leave-one-out predictions converge uniformly on compact sets. The arguments are technical and do not particularly impact the main thread of the paper, so we defer formal proofs to appendices.

#### Example 6.12 (The regression case).

In the case that we perform regression as in Section 2, we assume the existence of a population function $f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ , where the expectation is taken across environments, and $\widehat{f}_{-i}\to f$ for each $i$ . We assume this convergence is nearly uniform on compact sets: for each $\epsilon>0$ , there exists a subset $\mathcal{X}_{\epsilon}$ such that

$$ \sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\epsilon}}|\widehat{f}_{-i}(x)-f(x)|\mathop{\stackrel{{%
\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{\rightarrow}}}0~{}~{}\mbox{and}~{}~{}P(\mathcal{X}_{%
\epsilon})\geq 1-\epsilon. $$

Let $\lambda$ be Lebesgue measure. Then the locally uniform convergence condition (8) implies Assumptions 1.a and 2.c for $\lambda$ ; see Appendix C.2 for the argument.

Uniform convergence on compact sets is not a particularly onerous condition for standard problems. For example, for a linear regression model, if the estimate for model coefficients converges almost surely to the model coefficients, then assumption (8) holds trivially.

#### Example 6.13 (Quantile regression).

In the case of quantile-type regression problems, we recall Section 3.2.2, and we assume the consistency conditions that

$$ l(x)=\mathsf{Q}_{\alpha/2}(Y\mid X=x)~{}\mbox{and}~{}u(x)=\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha%
/2}(Y\mid X=x), $$

and that for each $x$ , $Y\mid X=x$ has a positive density, so that $l$ and $u$ are unique. Then in analogue to condition (8), we assume that for each $\epsilon>0$ , there exists $\mathcal{X}_{\epsilon}$ such that

$$ \sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\epsilon}}\max\left\{|\widehat{l}_{-i}(x)-l(x)|,|%
\widehat{u}_{-i}(x)-u(x)|\right\}\mathop{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{%
\rightarrow}}}0 $$

and

$$ P_{X}(\mathcal{X}_{\epsilon})\geq 1-\epsilon. $$

As in Example 6.12, if $\lambda$ is Lebesgue measure, then the convergence (9) implies Assumptions 1.a and 2.c for $\lambda$ . See Appendix C.3 for a proof.

#### Example 6.14 (Classification and logistic regression).

We consider a $k$ -class logistic regression problem, where we take the loss

$$ \ell(y,v)=\log\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}e^{v_{i}-v_{y}}\right)=\log\bigg{(}1+\sum_{i%
\neq y}e^{v_{i}-v_{y}}\bigg{)}. $$

We assume the predictors $f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{k}$ are (Bayes) optimal in that they satisfy

$$ \frac{\exp([f(x)]_{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\exp([f(x)]_{i})}=\mathbb{P}(Y=y\mid X=x). $$

As the loss $\ell$ is invariant to constant shifts we make the standing w.l.o.g. assumption that $f(x)$ and $\widehat{f}(x)$ are always mean zero (i.e. $\mathbf{1}^{T}f(x)=0$ ) and assume the consistency condition that for each $\epsilon>0$ , there exists $\mathcal{X}_{\epsilon}\subset\mathcal{X}$ such that

$$ \sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\epsilon}}\left\|{\widehat{f}_{-i}(x)-f(x)}\right\|%
\mathop{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{\rightarrow}}}0~{}~{}\mbox{and}~{}~{}P%
_{X}(\mathcal{X}_{\epsilon})\geq 1-\epsilon. $$

In this case, the uniqueness of quantile estimators requires a type of continuity condition that was unnecessary for the regression cases, and we make the additional continuity assumption that for each $c\in\mathbb{R}_{+}$ and $y\in[k]$ , the set $\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid\ell(y,f(x))=c\}$ has measure zero. As a consequence, the sets

$$ D_{c,\epsilon}\coloneqq\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid\mbox{there~{}exists~{}}y~{}%
\mbox{s.t.}~{}|\ell(y,f(x))-c|<\epsilon\right\} $$

satisfy $\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}P_{X}(D_{c,\epsilon})=0$ for each $c$ , by continuity of measure.

An analogous argument to that in Examples 6.12 and 6.13 then shows that the conditions above suffice for Assumptions 1.a and 2.c to hold with counting measure. See Appendix C.4.

### 6.2 Consistency of the multi-environment Jackknife-minmax

With the motivating examples in place, we now provide the main convergence theorem. We state one final assumption, which makes the environment-level quantiles sufficiently unique that identifiability is possible.

#### Assumption 3.

Define the quantile of the coverage threshold (7) on environment $i$ by

$$ \mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}(P^{i})\coloneqq\inf\left\{t\mid P^{i}(\tau(X,Y,C)\leq t)%
\geq 1-\alpha\right\}. $$

For a given $\delta$ , there exists a (unique) $q(\delta)$ such that for any $u>0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}(P^{E})\leq q(\delta)-u\right)<1-\delta, $$

and

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\mathsf{Q}_{1-\alpha}(P^{E})\leq q(\delta)+u\right)>1-\delta, $$

where the probability is taken over $E$ drawn randomly from $\mathcal{E}$ .

Given this assumption, we can show that the $X$ -measure of sets where the multi-environment jackknife-minmax and “true” confidence set $C_{\tau^{\star}(\delta,\alpha)}$ make different predictions converges to zero.

#### Theorem 6.15.

Let $\lambda$ be a measure on $\mathcal{Y}$ such that Assumptions 1.a, 2.c, and 3 hold. Let $\epsilon>0$ and $m=m(n)$ be a sufficiently slowly growing sequence. Then the $P_{X}$ measure of

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{B}(\epsilon)\coloneqq \displaystyle\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}~{}~{}\mbox{such that}~{}~{}\lambda\left(%
\widehat{C}^{\textup{jk-mmx}}_{m,\alpha,\delta}(x)\triangle C_{\tau^{\star}(%
\delta,\alpha)}(x)\right)\geq\epsilon\right\} $$

satisfies $P_{X}(\widehat{B}(\epsilon))\mathop{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{% \rightarrow}}}0$ .

#### Proof 6.16.

The key step in the argument is to recognize that Assumptions 1.a and 3 give consistency of the estimated threshold $\widehat{\tau}$ :

#### Lemma 6.17.

Let Assumption 1.a hold and 3 hold for the choice $\delta$ . Then for all suitably slowly growing sequences $m=m(n)\to\infty$ , the global estimated threshold $\widehat{\tau}\coloneqq\widehat{q}_{\delta}^{+}(\{S^{i}_{1-\alpha}\}_{i=1}^{m})$ in Algorithm 3.1 converges almost surely: $\widehat{\tau}\mathop{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{\rightarrow}}}q(\delta)$ .

We defer this proof to Section C.5, continuing with the main thread of the theorem.

Let $m=m(n)$ be a sequence tending to $\infty$ but such that the conclusions of Lemma 6.17 hold. Let $\widehat{\tau}=\widehat{q}_{\delta}^{+}(\{S^{i}_{1-\alpha}\}_{i=1}^{m})$ be the random $\delta$ -quantile in Alg. 3.1. Lemma 6.17 guarantees that $\widehat{\tau}\mathop{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{\rightarrow}}}q(\delta)$ . Following a slight variation of the notation of Assumption 2.c, define the sets $B_{n}^{i}=\{x\mid\lambda(\widehat{C}^{-i}_{\widehat{\tau}}(x)\triangle C_{\tau% ^{\star}(\delta,\alpha)}(x))\geq\epsilon\}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\left\{x\mid\lambda\left(\widehat{C}^{\textup{jk-mmx}}_{m,\alpha,%
\delta}(x)\triangle C_{\tau^{\star}(\delta,\alpha)}(x)\right)\geq\epsilon\right\} \displaystyle\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}B_{n}^{i} $$

and Assumption 2.c guarantees that the latter set has $P_{X}$ -measure tending to zero.

### 6.3 Consistency of multi-environment split conformal prediction

Similarly, we can show that the $X$ -measure of sets where the split conformal and “true” confidence set $C_{\tau^{\star}(\delta,\alpha)}$ make different predictions converges to zero.

#### Theorem 6.18.

Let $\lambda$ be a measure on $\mathcal{Y}$ such that Assumptions 1.b, 2.d, and 3 hold. Let $\epsilon>0$ and $m=m(n)$ be a sufficiently slowly growing sequence. Then the $P_{X}$ measure of

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{B}(\epsilon)\coloneqq \displaystyle\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}~{}~{}\mbox{such that}~{}~{}\lambda\left(%
\widehat{C}^{\textup{split}}_{m,\alpha,\delta}(x)\triangle C_{\tau^{\star}(%

#### Proof 6.19.
